# When Not to Use DataRaft {#sec-not-use}

Credible architecture includes a boundary. The question is not whether DataRaft can be inserted into a workflow. The question is whether its product, contract, quality, and evidence model is the simplest maintainable way to provide the guarantees that workflow needs.

## Use a plain script when the output is disposable

A one-off exploration with one author and no downstream dependency may not need a product identity, release history, or contract. Ordinary R code is easier to read and faster to change.

A useful transition point is recurrence. When the same analysis becomes a monthly delivery, when another person consumes it, or when a bad input becomes costly, the additional structure starts to pay for itself.

Do not make exploratory work imitate production before there is a production requirement.

## Prefer dbt when SQL already owns the transformation domain

If an organization is warehouse-centered, most transformations are SQL, teams already use dbt tests and documentation, and deployment is built around dbt, keep dbt at the center.

The experimental `dataraft.dbt` package can connect existing dbt projects and artifacts to DataRaft workflows where that adds value. It is not a reason to rewrite established SQL transformations in R.

A mixed architecture can be cleaner than a forced uniform one: dbt owns warehouse transformations, DataRaft owns a recurring R-side product or publication boundary, and the two exchange explicit artifacts.

## Prefer the managed platform when it already owns the lifecycle

A managed lakehouse or data platform may already provide contracts, quality gates, lineage, access control, deployment, release history, and operational tooling that fit the team's needs.

Adding a parallel DataRaft governance layer can create two sources of truth. In that situation, DataRaft may still be useful at a narrow R integration boundary, but it should not become the primary system of record merely for consistency.

The goal is not maximum use of DataRaft. It is minimum duplication of responsibility.

## Use distributed compute for distributed compute problems

DataRaft is not a distributed execution engine. It can work with supported lazy database-backed objects and delegate physical work, but it does not provide cluster scheduling, shuffle management, worker elasticity, or distributed fault tolerance.

If those are the dominant problem, use an engine designed for them. DataRaft can describe a checked interface around selected outputs if that is useful, but it should not sit in the critical compute path only to make the architecture look symmetrical.

## Be cautious when R is not part of the operating model

A product definition is most useful when the responsible team can read, test, and maintain it.

If production data engineering is entirely Python, SQL, JVM, or another ecosystem, introducing R solely to host governance definitions may create an additional language boundary without enough benefit. Open standards such as ODCS can be a better interchange point when authoring should remain outside R.

R-first is a strength only when R is genuinely part of the team's work.

## Do not use a contract to compensate for unclear ownership

A technically precise contract cannot decide who is responsible for a product, who may approve a breaking change, or who responds when a delivery fails. Metadata can record ownership; it cannot manufacture organizational accountability.

If no team owns the product, adding more checks may produce a better error message without producing a better operating model.

Resolve ownership and decision rights as part of platform design.

## Do not build a catalog before the definitions are worth discovering

A catalog is valuable when it exposes products with meaningful identity, ownership, descriptions, contracts, and lineage.

Publishing hundreds of vaguely defined tables into OpenMetadata does not turn them into data products. Start with good definitions. Add catalog integration when discovery across teams becomes a real problem.

The same rule applies to lineage visualization. A graph is useful when its nodes and edges represent understood product boundaries.

## Do not add a lake just because the word platform appears in the project

The book deliberately starts with in-memory execution and RDS releases. That path is not a toy architecture if it meets the required scale, concurrency, and recovery needs.

Move to `dataraft.lake` when its additional capabilities solve concrete problems such as shared release history, registry-backed discovery, recovery, integrity verification, lifecycle state, or lake-backed access.

Infrastructure should follow the required guarantees.

## A practical decision table

| Situation | Likely primary approach | Where DataRaft may fit |
|---|---|---|
| one-off R analysis | plain R script/notebook | probably nowhere yet |
| recurring R delivery with downstream users | DataRaft core + local target | primary product boundary |
| warehouse-first SQL transformation estate | dbt / warehouse tooling | R-side integration or governed publication |
| very large distributed transformation | distributed engine | interface around selected outputs |
| managed platform already covers governance | managed platform | only at an uncovered R boundary |
| R team needs contracts and quality but no platform services | DataRaft core | strong fit |
| R team needs retained governed releases | DataRaft + adapters/lake | strong fit if backend guarantees match |
| organization-wide semantic query layer | dedicated semantic system | metrics evidence may complement it |

This table is not a ranking of tools. It maps responsibilities to the systems designed to own them.

## The strongest fit

DataRaft is strongest when recurring R-centered data work has grown beyond a script but does not need, or cannot yet justify, a large platform.

Examples include:

- regulated or management reporting inputs;
- analytics data products produced in R;
- recurring model inputs and feature preparation;
- operational extracts with explicit consumer expectations;
- small data teams that need contracts and quality before they need a full control plane;
- platform teams that want an R-native product boundary around selected workflows.

In these cases, DataRaft provides a local path to explicit interfaces, acceptance decisions, diagnostics, evidence, and replaceable publication targets.

## The final design question

The book began with a data frame and a recurring script. It ends with a more precise question:

> Which guarantees do consumers need at this data boundary, and what is the smallest maintainable system that can provide them?

Sometimes the answer is a plain R script. Sometimes it is DataRaft. Sometimes it is dbt, a managed platform, a distributed engine, or a combination of systems.

The value of the DataRaft approach is not that every workflow becomes a DataRaft workflow. It is that when a recurring R delivery needs to become dependable, its meaning, acceptance rules, evidence, and physical realization can be made explicit without requiring the whole platform at once.

## Exercises

1. Evaluate three hypothetical teams: a single analyst with one monthly CSV, a SQL-first analytics team using dbt, and an R-heavy risk team producing governed recurring reports. Describe the simplest appropriate architecture for each.
2. Write a one-paragraph exit criterion for DataRaft: what future workload or organizational change would make you reconsider it as the primary product layer?
3. List the risks of adopting a development-stage package family and the controls you would require before using it for a critical production workflow.
